claim: Pristionchus pacificus nematodes produce an impressive diversity of structurally complex NDMMs.
source: Pristionchus pacificus nematodes produce an impressive diversity of structurally complex NDMMs, some of which act as primer pheromones that are capable of triggering irreversible developmental switches.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about P. pacificus.

claim: Some NDMMs produced by P. pacificus act as primer pheromones that are capable of triggering irreversible developmental switches.
source: Pristionchus pacificus nematodes produce an impressive diversity of structurally complex NDMMs, some of which act as primer pheromones that are capable of triggering irreversible developmental switches.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Many NDMMs found in P. pacificus have only ever been found in P. pacificus.
source: Many of these NDMMs have only ever been found in P. pacificus but no attempts have been made to study their evolution by profiling closely related species.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: This study identified 36 novel compounds through systematic MS/MS- and NMR-based analysis of exo-metabolomes from over 30 Pristionchus species.
source: We identified 36 novel compounds and found evidence for the convergent evolution of complex NDMMs in separate branches of the Pristionchus phylogeny.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: There is evidence for the convergent evolution of complex NDMMs in separate branches of the Pristionchus phylogeny.
source: We identified 36 novel compounds and found evidence for the convergent evolution of complex NDMMs in separate branches of the Pristionchus phylogeny.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by phylogenetic analyses and data in the results section.

claim: Biochemical innovation is a recurrent process in Pristionchus nematodes.
source: Our results demonstrate that biochemical innovation is a recurrent process in Pristionchus nematodes, a pattern that is probably typical across the animal kingdom.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the convergent evolution findings.

claim: The pattern of biochemical innovation observed in Pristionchus nematodes is probably typical across the animal kingdom.
source: Our results demonstrate that biochemical innovation is a recurrent process in Pristionchus nematodes, a pattern that is probably typical across the animal kingdom.
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation from the Pristionchus findings.

claim: Pheromonal signaling appears to be the most ancient and widespread form of communication used in the animal kingdom.
source: Pheromonal signaling appears to be the most ancient and widespread form of communication used in the animal kingdom (Agosta, 1992; Krieger and Breer, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Nematodes have long been known to communicate via pheromones.
source: Nematodes have long been known to communicate via pheromones, producing both releaser pheromones (those that trigger short-term behavioral responses, for example mate attraction) and primer pheromones (those that trigger long-term developmental responses, such as the production of quiescent dauer larvae) (Bone and Shorey, 1978; Golden and Riddle, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Nematodes produce both releaser pheromones and primer pheromones.
source: Nematodes have long been known to communicate via pheromones, producing both releaser pheromones (those that trigger short-term behavioral responses, for example mate attraction) and primer pheromones (those that trigger long-term developmental responses, such as the production of quiescent dauer larvae) (Bone and Shorey, 1978; Golden and Riddle, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Simple ascarosides consist of a 3,6-dideoxy-L-ascarylose sugar coupled to a fatty-acid-derived side chain.
source: Simple ascarosides consist of a 3,6-dideoxy-L-ascarylose sugar coupled to a fatty-acid-derived side chain (Jeong et al., 2005; Butcher et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a structural definition supported by citations.

claim: Nematodes produce hundreds of distinct NDMM molecules.
source: From this basic framework, nematodes produce hundreds of distinct molecules that are collectively referred to as nematode-derived modular metabolites (NDMMs).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Several NDMMs have been confirmed to influence aspects of behavior and development.
source: Several NDMMs have been confirmed to influence aspects of behavior (e.g., aggregation behavior in C. elegans) and development (e.g., control of the mouth-form polyphenism in P. pacificus) (Srinivasan et al., 2012; Bose, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NDMM production is widespread across the nematode phylum.
source: Targeted screening for known compounds confirmed that NDMM production is widespread across the nematode phylum (Choe et al., 2012), and earlier work identified long-chain ascarosides in the eggshells of parasitic Ascaris nematodes (Bartley et al., 1996), but there remains a need for unbiased biochemical screens that speak to the diversity of NDMMs present both within and across species.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: P. pacificus is a free-living soil nematode that is reliably found in association with scarab beetles.
source: P. pacificus is a free-living soil nematode that is reliably found in association with scarab beetles (Herrmann et al., 2006a; Herrmann et al., 2006b; Herrmann et al., 2007), and that has been developed as a model system in developmental genetics and comparative evolutionary biology.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: P. pacificus and C. elegans produce and use NDMMs in distinct ways.
source: Many studies in this species focused on two examples of phenotypic plasticity, and these efforts revealed that P. pacificus and C. elegans produce and use NDMMs in distinct ways.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from previous studies.

claim: P. pacificus exhibits mouth-form polyphenism with stenostomatous and eurystomatous forms.
source: The first example involves the development of the buccal cavity, with individuals adopting either the stenostomatous (St) mouth form with a single tooth, resulting in strict bacterial feeding, or the alternative eurystomatous (Eu) form with two teeth, which allows for predation on other nematodes (Bento et al., 2010; Bumbarger et al., 2013; Sieriebriennikov et al., 2017; Sieriebriennikov and Sommer, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The behavioral-morphological polyphenism in P. pacificus is broadly conserved within the Pristionchus genus and the larger Diplogastridae family.
source: This behavioral-morphological polyphenism is broadly conserved within the Pristionchus genus and the larger Diplogastridae family (Susoy et al., 2015), but is not found in non-Diplogastrids such as C. elegans.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Both mouth-form plasticity and dauer induction are sensitive to population density in P. pacificus.
source: Both mouth-form plasticity and dauer induction are sensitive to population density in P. pacificus, with NDMMs serving as chemical indicators of competitive environments in which predation or diapause represent adaptive survival strategies (Bento et al., 2010; Werner et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Completely different NDMMs are involved in the regulation of mouth-form plasticity and dauer induction in P. pacificus.
source: However, completely different NDMMs are involved in the regulation of these two plastic traits (Bose, 2012; Sommer and Mayer, 2015), and P. pacificus and C. elegans employ different NDMMs as molecular triggers for dauer entry (Bose, 2012; Schroeder, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: P. pacificus produces a surprising diversity of complex NDMMs that are not found in C. elegans.
source: Biochemical analysis of the P. pacificus exo-metabolome showed that this species produces a surprising diversity of complex NDMMs that are not found in C. elegans, including the dimeric NDMM dasc#1 and several highly modular compounds that are characterized by the presence of complex sidechains that incorporate intermediates from different primary metabolic pathways (the UBAS, PASC, and NPAR NDMMs) (Figure 1; Bose, 2012; Yim et al., 2015; Artyukhin et al., 2018; Falcke et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1.

claim: The common ancestor of P. pacificus and C. elegans existed around 100 million years ago.
source: However, the common ancestor of P. pacificus and C. elegans existed around 100 million years ago (Prabh et al., 2018; Werner et al., 2018b; Hong et al., 2019) and comparing just these two species can provide only limited insights into patterns of small molecule evolution in nematodes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: More than 40 Pristionchus species have been isolated from world-wide samplings of scarab beetles and other invertebrates.
source: This diversity includes more than 40 Pristionchus species that have been isolated from world-wide samplings of scarab beetles and other invertebrates (Kanzaki et al., 2012a; Kanzaki et al., 2012b; Kanzaki et al., 2012c; Yoshida et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pristionchus species fall into four major clades: the pacificus, maupasi, entomophagus, and triformis clades, plus an outgroup.
source: These Pristionchus species fall into four major clades—the pacificus, maupasi, entomophagus, and triformis clades—plus an outgroup (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), nearly all of which are culturable under laboratory conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Self-fertilizing hermaphroditism has evolved at least six times independently within the Pristionchus genus.
source: Although the majority of Pristionchus species are gonochoristic (comprised of males and females), self-fertilizing hermaphroditism has evolved at least six times independently within the genus, and the model species P. pacificus reproduces in this way (Rödelsperger et al., 2018; Weadick and Sommer, 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The study identified four simple NDMMs in P. pacificus: ascr#9, ascr#12, ascr#1, and part#9.
source: Consistent with previous studies, we identified four simple NDMMs in P. pacificus: the ascarosides ascr#9, ascr#12, and ascr#1, which form a homologous series with fatty acid side chains of differing length, and the paratoside part#9, which is similar to ascr#9 but which uses paratose as the sugar moiety in place of ascarylose.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Six additional simple NDMMs were found when examining other Pristionchus species: ascr#5, ascr#11, ascr#7, ascr#14, ascr#10 and ascr#18.
source: We found six additional simple NDMMs when examining other Pristionchus species: ascr#5 [asc-ωC3], ascr#11 [asc-C4], ascr#7 [asc-ΔC7], ascr#14 [asc-C8], ascr#10 [asc-C9] and ascr#18 [asc-C11] (Figures 2 and 3A; Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2; Supplementary file 3—Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis, supported by figures.

claim: ascr#1, ascr#9 and ascr#12 were produced by all species studied.
source: ascr#1, ascr#9 and ascr#12 were produced by all species, consistent with an ancient origin of these simple NDMMs (Figure 2 and Figure 2—source data 1; Supplementary file 1a—Figures 1–9).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis, supported by figures.

claim: ascr#7 was restricted to the entomophagus-clade.
source: By contrast, a few NDMMs, most notably ascr#7 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Supplementary file 1a—Figures 10–11) and part#9, were restricted to specific clades; ancestral reconstruction analyses suggest a single origin for ascr#7 along the branch that defines the entomophagus-clade, and two origins for part#9 within the pacificus-clade (Supplementary file 4—Figures 1–2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis and phylogenetic reconstruction.

claim: Ancestral reconstruction analyses suggest a single origin for ascr#7 along the branch that defines the entomophagus-clade.
source: By contrast, a few NDMMs, most notably ascr#7 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Supplementary file 1a—Figures 10–11) and part#9, were restricted to specific clades; ancestral reconstruction analyses suggest a single origin for ascr#7 along the branch that defines the entomophagus-clade, and two origins for part#9 within the pacificus-clade (Supplementary file 4—Figures 1–2).
evidence: This is a finding from phylogenetic reconstruction analyses.

claim: Ancestral reconstruction analyses suggest two origins for part#9 within the pacificus-clade.
source: By contrast, a few NDMMs, most notably ascr#7 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Supplementary file 1a—Figures 10–11) and part#9, were restricted to specific clades; ancestral reconstruction analyses suggest a single origin for ascr#7 along the branch that defines the entomophagus-clade, and two origins for part#9 within the pacificus-clade (Supplementary file 4—Figures 1–2).
evidence: This is a finding from phylogenetic reconstruction analyses.

claim: ascr#10 was absent from 6 of 7 hermaphroditic species but present in 23 of 25 gonochoristic species.
source: For example, ascr#10, a known attractant of C. elegans hermaphrodites (Izrayelit et al., 2012), was absent from 6 of 7 hermaphroditic species but present in 23 of 25 gonochoristic species, and was often produced by males at particularly high levels (Supplementary file 1a—Figures 12–24), suggesting a broadly conserved role as a sex pheromone in gonochoristic species (Figures 2 and 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: ascr#10 was often produced by males at particularly high levels in gonochoristic species.
source: For example, ascr#10, a known attractant of C. elegans hermaphrodites (Izrayelit et al., 2012), was absent from 6 of 7 hermaphroditic species but present in 23 of 25 gonochoristic species, and was often produced by males at particularly high levels (Supplementary file 1a—Figures 12–24), suggesting a broadly conserved role as a sex pheromone in gonochoristic species (Figures 2 and 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: ascr#10 has a broadly conserved role as a sex pheromone in gonochoristic Pristionchus species.
source: For example, ascr#10, a known attractant of C. elegans hermaphrodites (Izrayelit et al., 2012), was absent from 6 of 7 hermaphroditic species but present in 23 of 25 gonochoristic species, and was often produced by males at particularly high levels (Supplementary file 1a—Figures 12–24), suggesting a broadly conserved role as a sex pheromone in gonochoristic species (Figures 2 and 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the distribution and production patterns of ascr#10.

claim: ascr#10 was not detected in separate assays focused exclusively on P. pacificus males.
source: The lack of ascr#10 in hermaphroditic species might simply reflect the culture conditions (in which males are generally rare as the result of self-fertilization), but we note that ascr#10 was not detected in separate assays focused exclusively on P. pacificus males (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 4B), consistent with a total loss of ascr#10 biosynthesis in at least one hermaphroditic species.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: A food limitation (starvation) treatment altered NDMM levels in P. pacificus hermaphrodites.
source: Moreover, a food limitation (starvation) treatment altered NDMM levels in P. pacificus hermaphrodites, indicating that NDMM production rates are plastic (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: NDMM production by Pristionchus correlates with phylogeny in some respects but is also influenced by sex, the mode of reproduction, and the environment.
source: Combined, these results demonstrate high levels of species-specificity within the simple NDMM class and indicate that NDMM production by Pristionchus correlates with phylogeny in some respects but is also influenced by sex, the mode of reproduction, and the environment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings on simple NDMMs.

claim: PASC compounds were produced consistently by P. pacificus and its nine closest relatives.
source: PASC compounds were produced consistently by P. pacificus and its nine closest relatives, with pasc#9 being the most abundant compound in each case (Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1c—Figures 1–4).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: paso#9 includes a 4-hydroxyanthranilic acid moiety.
source: The production of paso#9 by P. pacificus was previously demonstrated by Artyukhin et al., 2018 but its structure was incompletely characterized; our NMR analysis indicated the presence of a 4-hydroxyanthranilic acid moiety in paso#9 (Figures 2 and 5D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 2b—Figure 1; Supplementary file 3—Table 14).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's NMR analysis.

claim: UBAS is produced by most members of the pacificus clade.
source: Our comparative screen uncovered several novel compounds and showed that UBAS is produced by most members of the pacificus clade, with a broader but patchier phylogenetic distribution than was seen for the PASC and NPAR classes (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's comparative screen.

claim: UBAS chemicals were unexpectedly found in triformis-clade species.
source: This prompted us to perform a targeted MS/MS screen (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D; Dong et al., 2016) that enabled the identification of a series of novel UBAS chemicals from pacificus-clade species and, unexpectedly, from triformis-clade species, including ubas#26 (which lacks a 2'-linked sidechain) and the dimeric UBASs ubas#27–#37 (defined by the presence of various 2'-linked ascaroside side chains) (Figures 2 and 4C; Supplementary file 3—Table 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's targeted MS/MS screen.

claim: Dimerization is an important mechanism for expanding the structural diversity of NDMMs.
source: These new discoveries, combined with our findings on DASC compounds (described above), highlight dimerization as an important mechanism for expanding the structural diversity of NDMMs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings on dimeric NDMMs.

claim: NPAR, PASC, and UBAS chemicals were not detected in the maupasi and entomophagus clades, nor in any of the outgroup Pristionchus species.
source: NPAR, PASC, and UBAS chemicals were not detected in the maupasi and entomophagus clades, nor were they found in any of the outgroup Pristionchus species (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's comparative analysis.

claim: UBAS and PASC compounds were found in members of the triformis clade.
source: However, UBAS and PASC compounds were unexpectedly also found in members of the triformis clade.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's comparative analysis.

claim: P. yamagatae produced pasc#9, pasc#12, and pasc#1.
source: With regard to PASC compounds, we found that P. yamagatae produced pasc#9, pasc#12, and pasc#1.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: P. triformis and P. hoplostomus produced a variety of monomeric UBAS NDMMs.
source: With regard to UBAS compounds, we found that P. triformis and P. hoplostomus produced a variety of monomeric UBAS NDMMs and that P. fukushimae produced a mixture of monomeric and dimeric compounds, some of which were entirely novel (Figures 2 and 4C; Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: P. fukushimae produced a mixture of monomeric and dimeric UBAS compounds, some of which were entirely novel.
source: With regard to UBAS compounds, we found that P. triformis and P. hoplostomus produced a variety of monomeric UBAS NDMMs and that P. fukushimae produced a mixture of monomeric and dimeric compounds, some of which were entirely novel (Figures 2 and 4C; Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Ancestral reconstruction analyses strongly suggest that neither PASC nor UBAS compounds were produced by the most recent common ancestor of the pacificus and triformis clades.
source: However, ancestral reconstruction analyses of both individual NDMMs and overall NDMM classes strongly suggest that neither PASC nor UBAS compounds were produced by this ancestral species (Figure 6A and Supplementary file 4—Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's phylogenetic analyses.

claim: PASC compounds evolved twice: once each within the pacificus and triformis clades.
source: Rather, PASC compounds were predicted to have evolved twice (once each within the pacificus and triformis clades), whereas UBAS was predicted to have evolved four times (once within the triformis clade and three times within the pacificus clade) (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's phylogenetic analyses.

claim: UBAS was predicted to have evolved four times: once within the triformis clade and three times within the pacificus clade.
source: Rather, PASC compounds were predicted to have evolved twice (once each within the pacificus and triformis clades), whereas UBAS was predicted to have evolved four times (once within the triformis clade and three times within the pacificus clade) (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's phylogenetic analyses.

claim: The study found evidence for the convergent evolution of highly modular PASC and UBAS NDMMs in the distantly related pacificus and triformis clades.
source: These analyses therefore argue for the convergent evolution of highly modular PASC and UBAS NDMMs in the distantly related pacificus and triformis clades.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phylogenetic analyses.

claim: The study uncovered a variety of simple and DASC NDMMs in non-Pristionchus diplogastrid species.
source: Doing so uncovered a variety of simple and DASC NDMMs, supporting the notion that these compounds originated prior to the establishment and diversification of the Pristionchus genus.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of outgroup species.

claim: Simple and DASC NDMMs originated prior to the establishment and diversification of the Pristionchus genus.
source: Doing so uncovered a variety of simple and DASC NDMMs, supporting the notion that these compounds originated prior to the establishment and diversification of the Pristionchus genus.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the presence of these compounds in outgroup species.

claim: NPAR, PASC, and UBAS chemicals were not detected in any of the assayed non-Pristionchus diplogastrid species.
source: However, NPAR, PASC, and UBAS chemicals were not detected in any of the assayed species, even at trace levels, indicating that these highly modular compounds are Pristionchus-specific evolutionary innovations.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of outgroup species.

claim: NPAR, PASC, and UBAS compounds are Pristionchus-specific evolutionary innovations.
source: However, NPAR, PASC, and UBAS chemicals were not detected in any of the assayed species, even at trace levels, indicating that these highly modular compounds are Pristionchus-specific evolutionary innovations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the absence of these compounds in outgroup species.

claim: D was significantly different from one for 21 of 35 compounds, indicating the presence of phylogenetic signal for most Pristionchus NDMMs.
source: D was significantly different from one for 21 of 35 compounds, indicating the presence of phylogenetic signal for most Pristionchus NDMMs (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's phylogenetic signal analysis.

claim: Pairwise phenotypic dissimilarities were significantly positively related to pairwise phylogenetic distances.
source: Pairwise phenotypic dissimilarities were significantly positively related to pairwise phylogenetic distances (Mantel test: Spearman's rho = 0.308; p=0.002); the relationship was linear at lower evolutionary scales but plateaued when pairwise distances involved the distantly related outgroup species (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's phylogenetic signal analysis.

claim: The intercept term for the linear fit of phenotypic dissimilarity versus phylogenetic distance was significantly greater than zero.
source: Notably, the intercept term for the linear fit was significantly greater than zero (95% CI = 0.354–0.433 when including outgroup comparisons, and 0.224–0.311 when ignoring outgroup comparisons; assuming independence among data points in both cases).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: A positive intercept implies that considerable phenotypic divergence is present at the point of speciation.
source: A positive intercept implies that considerable phenotypic divergence is present at the point of speciation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical finding.

claim: The study detected the presence of several novel NDMMs in Pristionchus exo-metabolomes at trace amounts, including one simple ascaroside, five DASC NDMMs, two UBAS NDMMs, and a novel NDMM class called UPAS.
source: However, we also detected the presence of several novel NDMMs in Pristionchus exo-metabolomes at unquantifiably low (trace) amounts, including one simple ascroside, five DASC NDMMs, two UBAS NDMMs, and a novel NDMM class that we refer to as UPAS (Supplementary file 3—Table 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's chemical analysis.

claim: UPAS chemicals carry a ureidopropionic acid moiety at the 4'-position of ascarylose instead of ureidoisobutyric acid.
source: When performing LC-ESI-(-)-MS/MS experiments, we observed a common fragment ion signal of C4H7N2O3–(m/z 131.0468, [M – H]–) (Figure 5—figure supplement 5), suggesting that these compounds carry a ureidopropionic acid moiety at the 4'-position of ascarylose instead of ureidoisobutyric acid.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's MS/MS analysis.

claim: UPAS chemicals were detected within the phylogenetically separated pacificus and triformis clades.
source: In summary, UPAS chemicals were, like UBAS NDMMs, detected within the phylogenetically separated pacificus and triformis clades, suggesting that they may be produced through a common biosynthetic pathway.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's comparative analysis.

claim: UPAS chemicals may be produced through a common biosynthetic pathway with UBAS NDMMs.
source: In summary, UPAS chemicals were, like UBAS NDMMs, detected within the phylogenetically separated pacificus and triformis clades, suggesting that they may be produced through a common biosynthetic pathway.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the similar distribution patterns of UPAS and UBAS.

claim: The core set of Pristionchus NDMMs consists of simple and DASC compounds.
source: First, the core set of Pristionchus NDMMs consists of simple and DASC compounds: simple NDMMs are produced by all studied species, whereas DASCs are produced by most, including multiple non-Pristionchus outgroup species, with multiple DASC compounds reconstructed at deep nodes within the Pristionchus phylogeny.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's comparative analysis.

claim: Pristionchus nematodes have expanded upon the core set of NDMMs in both lineage- and compound-specific ways.
source: Second, Pristionchus nematodes have expanded upon this core set of NDMMs in both lineage- and compound-specific ways.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The highly modular NPAR, PASC, and UBAS NDMMs all appear to be evolutionary innovations of the Pristionchus genus.
source: The highly modular NPAR, PASC, and UBAS NDMMs include various metabolic building blocks as accessory components that are attached to either the sugar or fatty acid moiety. These NDMMs all appear to be evolutionary innovations of the Pristionchus genus, being absent from outgroup Pristionchus species, other diplogastrids, and rhabditid nematodes such as C. elegans.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the absence of these compounds in outgroup species.

claim: Phylogenetic signal for Pristionchus NDMM presence or absence is largely the result of clade-specific enzymatic innovation.
source: This finding suggests that phylogenetic signal for Pristionchus NDMM presence or absence is largely the result of clade-specific enzymatic innovation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the patterns of phylogenetic signal.

claim: No two Pristionchus species (aside from the outgroup species P. paulseni and P. bucculentus) produce fully compatible sets of compounds.
source: The dynamic evolutionary patterns seen for the different NDMM classes result in considerable variability among species: aside from the outgroup species P. paulseni and P. bucculentus, no two Pristionchus species produce fully compatible sets of compounds.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's comparative analysis.

claim: The evolution of highly specific NDMM profiles across the genus involved a mixture of gradual change and rapid divergence.
source: Our results suggest that the evolution of highly specific NDMM profiles across the genus involved a mixture of gradual change and rapid divergence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phylogenetic analyses.

claim: The positive relationship between NDMM profile dissimilarity and phylogenetic distance appears to be largely linear.
source: On the one hand, the positive relationship between NDMM profile dissimilarity and phylogenetic distance appears to be largely linear (especially when discounting the divergent outgroup species), suggesting gradualism—as species became more evolutionarily distant, their NDMM profiles became less and less alike.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's phylogenetic analyses.

claim: The positive intercept term suggests that even young species pairs with negligible evolutionary distance would have distinct NDMM profiles.
source: On the other hand, the positive intercept term suggests that even young species pairs with negligible evolutionary distance would have distinct NDMM profiles.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical finding.

claim: Pristionchus nematodes clearly produce an impressive diversity of small molecules, including numerous highly modular compounds that have never before been discovered in nature.
source: Pristionchus nematodes clearly produce an impressive diversity of small molecules, including numerous highly modular compounds that have never before been discovered in nature.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: Most of the complex NDMMs found in Pristionchus presumably play some role in pheromonal communication.
source: Most of these compounds presumably play some role in pheromonal communication.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the nature of the compounds and their context.

claim: Competitive interactions in the decaying scarab beetle ecosystem may promote co-evolutionary pheromonal diversification in Pristionchus.
source: We suspect that competitive interactions in the decaying scarab beetle ecosystem, where Pristionchus worms compete for food and mating partners alongside many other chemically communicating species (including other ascaroside-producing nematodes), promote co-evolutionary pheromonal diversification, similar to that shown for insects and plants that also harbor high levels of secreted small-molecule diversity (Symonds and Elgar, 2008; Engl et al., 2018; Lombe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculation about the ecological drivers of NDMM diversification.

claim: Small molecules are, in general, rapidly evolving in nematodes, albeit with lineage-specific axes of structural diversification.
source: From this, we speculate that small molecules are, in general, rapidly evolving in nematodes, albeit with lineage-specific axes of structural diversification (Dong et al., 2016; Dong et al., 2018; Dolke et al., 2019; Bergame et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculation extrapolating from the Pristionchus findings to nematodes in general.

claim: Pristionchus nematodes provide an ideal system for exploring the mechanisms that drive the rapid and repeated evolution of small molecule architecture.
source: Pristionchus nematodes provide an ideal system for exploring the interrelated mechanisms—co-evolutionary ecology-driven processes on the one hand and the dynamics of genome and gene family evolution on the other—that drive the rapid and, in some cases, repeated evolution of small molecule architecture.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the value of the Pristionchus system.

claim: dasc#1 was detected from most Pristionchus species (24/32).
source: We detected dasc#1 from most Pristionchus species (24/32) alongside a number of additional DASC compounds that were formed from different simple ascarosides attached at either the 2'- or 4'-position of the ascarylose moiety (Figures 2 and 4A–B; Supplementary file 3—Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: DASC compounds were identified in 31 of 32 Pristionchus species.
source: All told, DASC compounds were identified in 31 of 32 species, suggesting that this NDMM class originated prior to the diversification of the Pristionchus genus (Supplementary file 4—Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: The DASC NDMM class originated prior to the diversification of the Pristionchus genus.
source: All told, DASC compounds were identified in 31 of 32 species, suggesting that this NDMM class originated prior to the diversification of the Pristionchus genus (Supplementary file 4—Figure 2).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the widespread distribution of DASC compounds.

claim: Most Pristionchus species produced multiple DASCs.
source: Most species produced multiple DASCs, among which dimers containing ascr#9 [asc-C5] and/or ascr#1 [asc-C7] were the most abundant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Dimers containing ascr#9 and/or ascr#1 were the most abundant DASCs.
source: Most species produced multiple DASCs, among which dimers containing ascr#9 [asc-C5] and/or ascr#1 [asc-C7] were the most abundant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: The abundance of dimers containing ascr#9 and/or ascr#1 is presumably due to the fact that these two precursors are produced at high levels in most species.
source: This pattern is presumably due, at least in part, to the fact that these two precursors are produced at high levels in most species (Figure 2 and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is an inference about the relationship between precursor abundance and dimer abundance.

claim: Four novel DASC chemicals harboring one or two units of ascr#7 are specific to species in the entomophagus clade.
source: Finally, we found four new dimeric ascarosides containing at least one ascr#7 [asc-ΔC7] unit, namely dasc#14 [4'-(asc-ΔC7)-asc-C5, 6], dasc#15 [4'-(asc-ΔC7)-asc-C6], dasc#16 [4'-(asc-ΔC7)-asc-C7, 7], and dasc#17 [4'-(asc-ΔC7)-asc-ΔC7, 8] (Figures 2 and 4B). These DASC compounds were exclusively detected in species from the entomophagus clade, the only group in which the ascr#7 precursor was found (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: The production of novel simple NDMMs can underlie the production of related modular compounds, demonstrating linked innovation at multiple structural levels.
source: These results show how the production of novel simple NDMMs (i.e., ascr#7, which is found only in the entomophagus clade) can underlie the production of related modular compounds, thereby demonstrating linked innovation at multiple structural levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings on ascr#7-containing DASCs.

claim: NPAR compounds were observed in the exo-metabolomes of P. pacificus and its six closest relatives.
source: NPAR compounds, which are distinguished by the presence of nucleoside- and amino acid-containing sidechains and by the use of paratose as the sugar scaffold, were observed in the exo-metabolomes of P. pacificus and its six closest relatives, with npar#1 typically present at the highest relative levels (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Seven of the eight pacificus-clade species that produce part#9 also produce NPAR NDMMs.
source: This distribution closely but imperfectly matches that of the NPAR precursor molecule, the simple paratoside part#9, with seven of the eight pacificus-clade species that produce part#9 also producing NPAR NDMMs.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Ancestral reconstruction analyses point to a single origin for NPAR compounds.
source: Ancestral reconstruction analyses point to a single origin for NPAR compounds that coincided with one of the two predicted origins for part#9, suggesting that part#9 production is a necessary but not sufficient condition for NPAR production in Pristionchus nematodes (Figure 6A and Supplementary file 4 - Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's phylogenetic analyses.

claim: part#9 production is a necessary but not sufficient condition for NPAR production in Pristionchus nematodes.
source: Ancestral reconstruction analyses point to a single origin for NPAR compounds that coincided with one of the two predicted origins for part#9, suggesting that part#9 production is a necessary but not sufficient condition for NPAR production in Pristionchus nematodes (Figure 6A and Supplementary file 4 - Figure 2).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the phylogenetic analyses.

claim: dasc#5 [4'-(asc-C5)-asc-C5, 3] is specific to species in the maupasi clade.
source: For example, LC-ESI-(+)-MS/MS fragmentation of dasc#3 [2'-(asc-C5)-asc-C4, 1], detected in P. degawai and P. fukushimae (Figures 2 and 4A), afforded an ion signal of C17H28NaO8+ (m/z 383.1667, [M + Na]+, Δ 2.4 ppm) with a loss of the C4 side chain (Supplementary file 2a—Figure 1), which helped to assign the first and the second ascarosides as ascr#9 [asc-C5] and ascr#11 [asc-C4], respectively (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B for details on the nomenclature of DASC chemicals). Subsequent analysis of the dqf-COSY spectrum of dasc#3 (1) from P. fukushimae corroborated these assignments and further demonstrated that ascr#9 was connected to the 2'-position of ascr#11 (Supplementary file 1b—Figure 1 and Supplementary file 3—Table 7). Interestingly, we found that two ascr#9 units can be linked at the 2'- or 4'-position, resulting in two isomers, dasc#4 [2'-(asc-C5)-asc-C5, 2] (Figures 2, 4A and 5A; Supplementary file 3—Table 8) and dasc#5 [4'-(asc-C5)-asc-C5, 3] (Figures 2, 4A and 5B; Supplementary file 3—Table 9), the latter of which displayed a high specificity to nematodes of the maupasi clade (Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.
